title: Confession recorded by NDPS officers - admissibility after recent rulings
p1:
Can a confession recorded by a Narcotics Control Bureau officer send someone to prison? The Supreme Court's answer may surprise you.

Many people assume that if an accused voluntarily admits involvement in a drug-related offence before an NDPS officer, that statement can automatically be used as evidence.
p2:
But the law says otherwise.

In Tofan Singh v. State of Tamil Nadu (2020), the Supreme Court settled a crucial question: officers empowered under Section 53 of the NDPS Act are treated as police officers for this purpose. Consequently, a confession made to them is barred under Section 25 of the Evidence Act.

More importantly, a statement recorded under Section 67 of the NDPS Act cannot be used as a confessional statement to convict an accused.
p3:
The Supreme Court reaffirmed this position in subsequent decisions, including Rajkumar Hariram Gameti v. State of Gujarat (2024).

Here's the practical takeaway: signing a statement or allegedly admitting guilt before an NDPS officer does not automatically make that confession admissible in court. The prosecution must establish its case through legally admissible evidence, not simply rely on a Section 67 confession.

This distinction can make a significant difference in criminal trials.
conclusion: Do you think excluding confessions recorded by NDPS officers provides an essential safeguard against forced admissions, or does it make drug-related investigations more difficult? Share your perspective.
